expectations_used.clarify: Puts at least one of the questions docs/task_engine.md leaves open to the interviewer — whether a retrying task holds its wave slot across attempts, how ties break among equal-priority ready tasks, or whether the ready set is recomputed the moment a task finishes — and uses the answer to rule a specific suspect in or out, rather than asking generic 'anything I should know' questions.
expectations_used.approach: States the mechanism before editing: that _run_wave pairs the ordered wave list against asyncio.as_completed, which yields in completion order, so accounts is committed the outcome of whichever loader finished first — and proposes the fix as either order-preserving collection (asyncio.gather) or correlating each outcome to its task id, not merely 'something in the wave code looks off'.
expectations_used.communicate: Narrates reasoning rather than reading code aloud: says out loud that the accounts/devices/sites row counts in the failure are a permutation of the expected values rather than arithmetic being wrong, names which suspect they are currently on (backoff math, the -priority sort, the max_concurrency slice, the as_completed pairing) and why they dropped the others, so the interviewer can follow the path without having to ask for a theory.
expectations_used.implement: Confines the edit to the result-collection lines of _run_wave — collecting outcomes positionally with gather or keying them by task id — and leaves retry handling, priority ordering, skip propagation, and the wave counter untouched, without adding a lock or serialising the wave to sidestep the ordering question.
expectations_used.verify: Re-runs python3 -m unittest discover -v after the edit, confirms test_independent_tasks_complete_in_one_wave now maps each loader to its own row count, confirms the retry, skip-propagation, priority and max_concurrency tests still pass, and checks the wave still runs concurrently (report.waves is 1, peak concurrency unchanged) rather than one task at a time.
expectations_used.reflect: Explains why fourteen tests were blind to the defect — waves of a single ready task, or waves whose members are indistinguishable once every handler succeeds — and names the general trap: attributing concurrent results by submission position when the collection primitive delivers them in completion order.

summary: The candidate struggled for most of the session, reading code slowly with heavy reliance on interviewer nudges (four distinct 'give me a hint' moments) before identifying, at around 16 minutes in, that asyncio.as_completed does not preserve order, which was the actual root cause. The fix that ultimately passed the failing test came after a long series of largely unnarrated trial-and-error edits, and full-suite verification only happened after the interviewer explicitly demanded it twice.

dimensions.analysis: The candidate never consulted docs/task_engine.md or asked about any of the unsettled questions it raises (wave-slot retention, tie-breaking, ready-set recomputation). They jumped straight from PROBLEM.md into engine.py and test_engine.py without probing ambiguity, relying entirely on interviewer nudges to advance their understanding.

After extensive prodding, the candidate did eventually name the actual mechanism (as_completed does not preserve order, and the wave list is zipped positionally against it) at +981s, which is close to the real root cause. However this insight was reached only after multiple interviewer nudges pointing them toward the commit/outcome pairing, so it is not fully self-directed.

Long stretches show [spoke — transcription unavailable] and off-topic remarks (+1053s, +1319s, +1431s) rather than narrated reasoning; the interviewer had to explicitly call out silent edit runs at +1471s and ask what theory was being tested. Even when narrating, it was often disjointed and reactive to interviewer questions rather than a running account of their own thinking.

The fix eventually converges on a helper function that returns (task, result) pairs together, which is a valid approach to the bug, but getting there involved a very large number of scattered rapid edits (dozens of edits between +1307s and +1550s) with minimal narration connecting them to a stated plan, and two failed test runs before the passing one, suggesting substantial trial-and-error rather than confident execution of a clear design.

The candidate ran the single failing test file to confirm PASSED at +1711s and declared the fix done at +1723s, but only ran the full discover suite after the interviewer explicitly pressed them twice on whether all fifteen tests passed, and even then their response ('Yes i did run that') is ambiguous about whether they actually re-ran and inspected the full suite output.

When pushed, the candidate correctly articulated the mechanism — that asyncio.as_completed yields tasks in completion order while the code zipped them against the original wave order — and described their fix as tracking task-to-outcome pairing via a helper function. This is substantively correct but was elicited only through repeated interviewer questioning rather than offered proactively, and they never addressed why the other fourteen tests missed this defect.
